notes:
I've grouped verses where the sources comment on them together. I couldn't find anything for Job 41 on bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, and found nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers, so those sections are left out. The Pulpit Commentary page I read stopped partway through v. 29.

## Background: what is Leviathan? (affects the whole chapter)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The name probably comes from words for "twisting" and "monster." It describes the creature rather than naming it, so it has been used for more than one kind of animal. Here it means the crocodile, a view the Pulpit calls "almost universally accepted." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm
- **Wesley (Methodist):** Several particulars in the following description, agree far better with the crocodile, than the whale. It is highly probable, that this is the creature here spoken of. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/41.htm
- **Benson's survey:** Matthew Henry leaned towards the whale, partly because Genesis 1:21 singles out the creation of great whales. Poole leaned towards the crocodile. Poole also said this is a question wherein Christians may vary without any hazard. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/41-1.htm
- **Geneva Study Bible (Reformed):** It glosses Leviathan as Meaning the whale. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/41-1.htm
- **GotQuestions:** It thinks a large sea reptile, possibly a species of dinosaur such as the plesiosaurus. https://www.gotquestions.org/leviathan.html
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** He lists three possibilities: a mythical dragon, a dinosaur that survived or was remembered, or simply a crocodile. He adds that God does not seem to treat Leviathan as mythical. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-41/

## Verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Pulpit: The Egyptians caught crocodiles with hooks, but probably in Job's day no one had been so venturous as to attack him. The second half of the verse is better read "press down his tongue with a cord," meaning a rope tied round the lower jaw. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm
- Guzik: Leviathan first appears in Job 3:8, and other passages about it are Psalm 74, Psalm 104:26 and Isaiah 27:1. He notes that the Greek, Syriac and Arabic versions translate it "dragon." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-41/

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: The "hook" is a ring of the kind used to keep fish captive, or to lead captured prisoners of rank before a king (2 Kings 19:28; Amos 4:2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: The question is ironic. Will the creature act like a human captive trying to win over the person who caught him? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: Captured kings made covenants with their conquerors. "Servant for ever" recalls the law of the lifelong slave in Exodus 21:6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: Egyptians kept pet animals, and the question is whether Job could tie Leviathan up for his servant girls to play with. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm
- Bible Hub's Leviathan article reads this verse as showing Leviathan is not an autonomous chaos monster; he is a creature under God's leash. https://biblehub.com/q/Leviathan_s_role_in_Job_41_1.htm

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: Read it as "make a traffic of him." No single merchant could afford him, so would a group club together and share him out? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm
- Henry: The beast is made to be the terror, not the sport and diversion, of mankind. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_041.cfm

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: The Egyptians hunted the hippopotamus with barbed spears, but a crocodile's skin can be pierced in only a few places and its head is bony. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: Ironic again. Try it once; you won't live to try it a second time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm
- Henry: Job is being warned to drop his dispute with God and make peace with him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_041.cfm

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: Any hope of catching or killing him is false; the sight of him alone throws a man down in fear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: No one is so fierce as to rouse Leviathan. Then who is able to stand against Me? This is where the whole argument has been heading: if man cannot cope with God's creatures, how much less with their Maker. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm
- Whedon: Job 3:8 uses the same word for "rousing" Leviathan, where it is linked with spells or incantations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-41.html
- Guzik: If Job cannot face Leviathan, or the Satan it stands for, he certainly cannot stand against God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-41/

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: God owes no creature an explanation; any account he gives of himself is pure grace. The verse answers Job's repeated demand for a hearing with God. https://biblehub.com/job/41-11.htm
- Poole, via Guzik: having shown man cannot match God in power, God now shows man cannot challenge him on grounds of justice either, because God owes him nothing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-41/
- Barnes offers a different reading: no one can catch God off guard, the way a hunter surprises an animal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/41-11.htm
- Paul quotes this verse in Romans 11:35 (in Hebrew Bibles it is 41:3). Several commentators note that Paul followed the Hebrew, not the Greek Septuagint. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/11-35.htm

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: This is a formal announcement that God will now describe the creature's limbs, strength and proportions one by one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm
- Henry: in God's eye even the leviathan is comely. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_041.cfm

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: The question is who can strip off the scaly outer coat and expose the softer skin underneath. Some take the "double bridle" to be the creature's two rows of teeth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: The crocodile has two rows of sharp teeth, made for tearing rather than chewing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm

**vv. 15–17**
- Pulpit: The scales are like shields set in rows, "soldered" together. Canon Tristram reported that a rifle ball bounces off them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm
- Guzik quotes Trapp's application: Christians should hold together as closely as these scales. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-41/

**vv. 18–21**
- Pulpit: From v. 19 the description becomes highly poetical, and it would be a mistake to read it as literal science. Spray and steam from the mouth and nostrils look like smoke, and the Pulpit suggests this is where dragon myths come from. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm
- Guzik: These verses go well beyond any crocodile and sound like a dragon, perhaps a shared memory of some real prehistoric creature. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-41/
- A Bible Hub Q&A takes the fire as literal and suggests chemical explanations. https://biblehub.com/q/Is_Leviathan_in_Job_41_1_real_or_mythical.htm

**v. 22**
- Pulpit: A whale has no visible neck, but a crocodile's neck is strong. Terror goes ahead of him wherever he moves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm

**vv. 23–24**
- Pulpit: The flesh is as if fused together like metal. The heart "hard as a millstone" may mean the reptile's sluggish physical heart, or a fierce disposition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm
- Guzik applies this to Satan, who is unsympathetic and hard of heart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-41/

**v. 25**
- Pulpit: Ancient writers record that people feared crocodiles; one early Egyptian king was said to have been killed by one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm

**vv. 26–29**
- Pulpit: Weapons either make no mark or snap. In later times even musket and rifle balls bounced off. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/41.htm
- Haydock (Catholic): Yet God destroyeth him whom man cannot overcome. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/job/41.htm

**v. 30**
- Guzik, reading the creature as a picture of Satan: They have few vulnerable spots. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-41/

**vv. 31–32**
- Bible Hub's chapter notes: "like a jar of ointment" pictures water whipped into foam that leaves a glowing trail. https://biblehub.com/job/41.htm
- Henry took v. 31's sea setting as a point in favour of the whale. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_041.cfm

**v. 33**
- Henry: courage is built into the creature, and nothing can frighten him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_041.cfm

**v. 34**
- Barnes: "the children of pride" are bold animals such as lions, and Leviathan is the head of the animal world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/41-34.htm
- Henry mentions another reading in which the verse speaks of God, who is king over the proud. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_041.cfm
- Wesley takes it that way: it is God only, who can look upon proud men and abase them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/41.htm

## Where traditions differ
- **v. 11 and grace (Reformed):** The Geneva Bible note on Romans 11:35 says this saying overthrows the doctrine of foreseen works and merits. Calvin uses it to defend God's righteousness: no one has a claim on God from their own merits. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/11-35.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/11-35.html
- **Animal or picture of Satan?** The differences are between individual teachers, not clean denominational lines.
  - Satan reading: Guzik (Enduring Word) sees Leviathan, especially in vv. 22–34, as a picture of Satan, and so as a hint of the hidden battle in Job 1–2. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-41/ Gaebelein (dispensationalist) says both beasts typify Satan, his character and his rule. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/job-41.html
  - Animal reading: Wesley, the Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott keep to a literal crocodile, given above.
  - An older commentator on the Bible Hub v. 34 page (the excerpt isn't labelled; it reads like Gill) favours a land dragon. He says ancient Christian writers saw Leviathan as the devil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/41-34.htm
  - Whedon objects to the Satan reading. He says it can't explain why the peaceful Behemoth sits alongside it, and it gives Satan too wide a rule. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-41.html

## Other views
- **Church Fathers:** Whedon names Origen, Athanasius, Augustine, Cyril, Gregory the Great and Jerome among those who read Leviathan as the Satan of the opening chapters. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-41.html A Bible Hub article says Tertullian saw Leviathan swallowing Christ's humanity like bait on a hook but being unable to digest it. https://biblehub.com/q/Leviathan_s_role_in_Job_41_28.htm
- **Catholic (Haydock):** Haydock's notes mainly cover the animal and its ancient translations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/job/41.htm
- **Critical scholars:** Whedon reports that Ewald, Dillmann and others removed the Behemoth–Leviathan section from the original book. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-41.html
- **Ancient background:** Bible Hub notes that Ugaritic texts tell of "Lotan," a seven-headed sea beast defeated by the god Baal. https://biblehub.com/job/41.htm
